n: The king and a shaken Haman arrive at Esther’s second banquet. The moment of truth has come.

f.g: Literally “to drink” — to the wine feast.

n: For the third time the king asks Esther’s request and promises up to half his kingdom.

f.w: even to the half of the kingdom

n: Esther finally speaks: spare my life, and spare my people. In one sentence she reveals that she belongs to the people under the death sentence.

f.w: let my life be given me
f.g: A plea for her own life — now openly tying herself to her people.

n: She quotes the decree’s own words — destroy, slay, perish. If it were only slavery, she would not have troubled the king. Her careful wording shows respect while exposing the horror.

f.w: to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish

n: The king, apparently not realizing he approved this, demands to know who would dare do such a thing.
Esther points to him: “this wicked Haman.” Haman is struck with terror before the king and queen.
The furious king storms out to the garden, perhaps to think about how he was manipulated. Haman stays to beg the queen for his life — he knows the king has decided against him.
When the king returns, Haman has thrown himself on Esther’s couch begging for mercy. The king accuses him of assaulting the queen. Servants cover Haman’s face — a sign of condemnation.

f.g: The couch on which Esther reclined at the meal.
A sign that he was condemned to die.

n: Harbonah, a palace attendant, mentions the 75-foot gallows Haman built for Mordecai — the man who saved the king’s life. The king orders, “Hang him on it.”

f.w: who had spoken good for the king

n: Haman dies on the very gallows he built for Mordecai. The scriptures often teach that the wicked fall into the traps they set for others.

f.w: the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai
